newsitem.title: UK: No respite for dlr/yen in Europe, mark/yen crashes.
newsitem.headline: No respite for dlr/yen in Europe, mark/yen crashes.

text.p: The dollar slumped against the yen in Europe on Friday for the ninth consecutive day as a relentless scramble to buy back Japanese yen continued amid sudden paranoia about higher Japanese interest rates.
Analysts said the market focus is almost entirely on the recovery of the yen and this is illustrated by the stability of dollar/mark and the consequent slide in the mark/yen cross to 20-month lows.
Traders took advantage of a bout of short-covering in Tokyo at more attractive levels to cover long-standing short-yen positions and a modest dollar bounce was capped at 117.
"What this relentless push lower shows us is the sheer weight of short-yen positions that have yet to be covered," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas.

"The Japanese and the U.S., however, will have an interest in underpinning the dollar under 115 - not least because it's starting to hurt U.S. Treasuries," said Parsons. "The deep irony is that just a couple of weeks after Japan was theatening to sell dollar/yen they may now be forced to buy it."
At 1110 GMT, the dollar was trading at 115.65/70 yen, down more than half a yen from the close in Europe on Thursday and down more than a full yen from the overnight high at 117.00.
The dollar/yen has collapsed from 4-1/2-year highs this month and lost almost 10 percent of its value in just two weeks.

The reversal was triggered by a barrage of verbal intervention from Japanese officials aimed at preventing the yen from weakening further and hastening the need for higher Japanese interest rates. Growing speculation about a rise in Japanese rates, nevertheless, has reinforced the yen recovery.

The Bank of Japan declined comment on an overnight news agency report it was not concerned about the pace of the yen's recent retreat. However, the report was enough to rein in a mild dollar bounce in Tokyo.
Japanese vice Finance Minister Takatoshi Kato said later the Group of Seven industrialised nations accord on preventing excessive foreign exchange movements had now been fully absorbed by the market.

Analysts said this was code for saying the initially desired recovery of the yen has gone far enough. However, Kato kept the prospect of higher interest rates alive by saying the economic recovery was intact and private demand was rising.
The yen surge and rising Japanese rates have prompted a retreat of both Japanese capital and yen-funded capital around the world, sending many emerging currencies sharply weaker.
The mark remains subdued against the dollar as there is little or no pressure for higher European interest rates.
The drive to meet strict budgetary targets for European monetary union is forcing European authorities to keep a tight rein on fiscal policy and not monetary policy.

"The German budget news shows Germany may well miss the EMU entry criteria but the political statements indicate they will start EMU anyway," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago. "This is raising speculation of a broad-based start to the single currency and that the euro will be a softer unit."
